scenes.text: You were born with almost one hundred more bones than you have right now.
A newborn baby has around two hundred seventy-five to three hundred bones.
Most adults have just two hundred and six.
So where do the extra bones go? They don't disappear.
Many baby bones start out as cartilage, a tough but rubbery tissue.
As children grow, that cartilage hardens into bone, in a process called ossification.
And many smaller bones slowly fuse together into bigger ones.
Your skull is a great example.
At birth, a baby's skull isn't one solid piece, it's made of several separate bones.
Between them are soft spots called fontanelles.
This lets the skull change shape slightly during birth.
The soft spots usually close within the first year or two of life.
Most fusing is done around puberty, but your collarbone may not finish until your early to mid twenties.
Even in adults, bones are living tissue that keeps rebuilding itself.
Bonus fact: your hands and feet hold more than half of all your bones.
Each hand has twenty-seven bones, and each foot has twenty-six.
Did you know you used to have more bones?

title: You were born with almost 100 more bones 🦴
caption: Newborns have about 275-300 bones, adults have 206. The extra ones don't vanish: they fuse together as you grow.
